messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Hector was sixty-two when the car hit him. He had been driving home after a late rehearsal with the contemporary dance company where he had worked for thirty years, exhausted but satisfied. The other driver ran a red light and T-boned Hector’s sedan at an intersection he had crossed a thousand times. He remembers the screech of tires, the shattering of glass, the smell of gasoline—but when he tries to tell anyone what happened, the words jam. He can’t put the event into language; what stays is the sound, the physical shock, and a burning shame that he now associates with the wreck itself. He came to believe that the collision happened because of the sort of person he is: reckless, weak, not careful enough. In the months that followed, as his broken ribs healed and a torn rotator cuff slowly allowed him to lift his arm again, he began to feel that he would never be able to feel normal emotions—that something inside him had been permanently flattened.

To manage the intrusive sounds that rose up unexpectedly during the day—the squeal of brakes, the crunch of metal—Hector tried hard not to think about the trauma at all. He deliberately tried to blank out or leave his body when a memory threatened to surface, especially during rehearsals when the music and movement left him vulnerable. At night he stayed up until very late, delaying sleep, because lying in the dark was when the auditory fragments were most insistent. These strategies gave him a fragile sense of control, but they also deepened his conviction that he was helpless—that he couldn't stop bad things from happening, not then and not now. Each time he suppressed a thought or dissociated, the shame on recall grew stronger, and he believed more firmly that his character was fundamentally flawed.

In the studio, Hector started scanning for exits as soon as he entered any room or building. Every doorway, every fire escape became a silent preoccupation. He would notice them while warming up at the barre, while watching the choreographer mark counts. When a partner touched him unexpectedly during a lift, he reacted with alarm—a flinch that startled them both. The constant sense of danger that shadowed his every moment in the studio was, for him, the most convincing proof that he had become a fundamentally broken person, incapable of recovering the man he used to be. These threat responses were fed by his appraisals: he was certain he could not stop another catastrophe, that his emotions were gone forever, and that he deserved whatever came his way. At the same time, feeling constantly on edge brought the memory of the crash rushing back: the sound of the impact, the hot flood of shame, the inability to describe it. He found himself trapped in a cycle where scanning for danger and flinching at touch triggered vivid auditory intrusions, and those intrusions made him more vigilant.

His attempts to dissociate and suppress did not free him. When he deliberately blanked out during a rehearsal, the memories often returned later with greater intensity—the screech, the shame—pushing him to stay up later, to avoid sleep altogether. This pattern only reinforced his belief that he would never recover his capacity for normal feeling, and that his helplessness was a permanent part of who he was. The more he tried not to think, the more the nonverbal fragments forced their way in, and the more convinced he became that the crash had revealed his true, broken self.

Hector is still dancing, but he now avoids certain partnering passages that require close physical contact. He has stopped staying after rehearsal for colleagues’ company, preferring to leave the studio alone so he can scan the parking lot for a full minute before getting into his car. His marriage has suffered: his wife tries to comfort him and he startles, and the shame afterwards leaves him silent. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment during a performance last month when a dancer brushed against him unexpectedly—he felt his body go rigid, heard the sound of shattering glass in his head, and nearly walked off the stage mid-show. He is terrified that his career is crumbling, and that the person he used to be—the dancer, the husband—is gone. All he hopes for is to feel something other than fear.
